title: Two riddles and an onion
about: Peer Gynt is a peasant widow’s son in Norway, known for his tall tales. In Act 2 he asks the troll king, the Old Man of the Dovrë, for his daughter and his kingdom, and the Old Man tests him with a riddle. In Act 5 Peer comes home old and shipwrecked, and a Button-Moulder is waiting to melt him down as a man who has never been himself. Solveig, the girl he left in Act 3, has waited in the forest hut all that time.

view.says: In February 1941, the year of the course, Auden wrote that every answer is provisional: Solveig’s settles no more than the earlier ones, and Peer has the Button-Moulder still to meet. In *The Dyer’s Hand* he reads Peer as the poet, for whom almost everything he does is a part to play.
view.quote: Throughout Peer Gynt, one question keeps being asked and answered in various ways, namely, Who am I? What is my real self?
view.source: “Genius & Apostle,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 436 and 438; “The Wandering Jew,” *The New Republic*, 10 February 1941; reprinted in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 110–13
view.checked: The Dyer’s Hand read in the scan, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 20646-20648 (p. 436; the scan misprints two words of the sentence quoted, which is given here as in the research notes) and lines 20730-20734 (p. 438), read again on 2026-10-03. Examiner, 2026-10-03: both pages read again in the scan (the page number stands at the head of its page); the role sentence is on p. 438. The review of 1941 is not among the scans. Its sentence on Solveig’s answer and the Button-Moulder was seen as the passage that an exact-phrase search of archive.org returns from the scanned issue of The New Republic (vol. 104, no. 1367, 10 February 1941; the contents list the review at p. 185) and from the scanned Prose volume; the sentence that all the answers are provisional and salvation left in doubt was seen the same way. The page numbers in Prose, vol. II are those of remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 17 and H17b. Not seen in full.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.why: The two sayings are built alike, and in Ibsen the commands differ by one added word; the Old Man himself calls it the sundering word.
lenses.caption: The Old Man sets Peer a riddle: what is the difference between a troll and a man. He answers it himself with two sayings, each with a place, the same frame (the saying goes), a name called out and a command. Contrasted things set side by side in matching form are called antithesis. In Ibsen the trolls’ command is the men’s three words with one more after a dash, and that word is the whole difference between the two commands. The translators, William and Charles Archer, also add a to and turn two words round. In his next speech the Old Man calls the added word sundering, dividing.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, which includes the Old Man’s next speech. The riddle is put a few lines earlier in [Act 2, scene 6](#/read/peer-gynt/a2s6:36). Antithesis as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Ibsen’s Norwegian in the Oslo edition, *Henrik Ibsens skrifter*, with *Bokmålsordboka* for the added word.

grounds.claim: the two sayings match part for part; in the English the second command has the two words of the first turned round after to, then a dash and one more word; in his next speech (rows 49.0-49.1) the Old Man names the added word and calls it sundering

grounds.source: Act 2, scene 6 (a2s6): rows 36.0-36.1, 38.0 and 40.0; rows 42.2-42.3 on the plate

grounds.claim: antithesis: contrasted words or ideas placed side by side, often in matching form

points.say: The last beat falls here, and the line and the saying end together.
The same word now has the last beat but one. The last falls after the dash, on the added word.
Two beats. Peer’s reply has the other two: the courtier and Peer share one line.
The noun begins its line with a beat, after the two adjectives that end the line before. Ibsen divides the lines the same way, and his line end there is a rhyme word.

lenses.why: The Archers keep Ibsen’s four beats and line ends without his rhymes: the men’s saying ends on thyself, the trolls’ on the added word, a rhyme word in Ibsen; rhyme emphasizes the end of a line.
lenses.caption: The Archers’ translation gives up Ibsen’s rhymes and keeps his measure, line for line: four beats, here with one or two syllables between them. The rule under each line marks the beats; the dots are the speaking voice. In the men’s saying the last beat falls on thyself and the line ends. In the trolls’ saying thyself has the last beat but one, and the last comes after the dash, on the added word. In Ibsen both line ends are rhyme words, and a handbook of verse says that rhyme emphasizes the end of a line. The added word is given that place.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. William Archer’s Introduction to the translation, on its verse. Ibsen’s rhyme words and line ends in the Oslo edition, *Henrik Ibsens skrifter*. Rhyme and the end of the line: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 3.

lenses.why: Enough means sufficient; for Auden, to be enough to oneself is to have no I set over against the self, and he applies the word to the poet, who as a poet manages without other people.
lenses.caption: Enough means as much as is needed. The Old Man calls it a sundering word, one that divides, to be cut on Peer’s escutcheon, the shield with his coat of arms. Auden, quoting both sayings in The Enchafèd Flood, says that to be enough to oneself is to have no conscious I set over against the self: one cannot refuse oneself, tell fantasy from fact, or lie. In The Dyer’s Hand he applies the word to the poet, who as a poet manages without other people. In Act 5 the word alone is Peer’s reply; a few lines on he says it again with two names: a hill-troll, an egoist.
lenses.stands: The Online Etymology Dictionary under *enough*, *sunder* and *escutcheon*. The Norwegian phrase in *Bokmålsordboka*, under *nok*; Ibsen’s word in the Oslo edition. The Old Man’s words in the passage, and Peer’s a few lines after his reply in [Act 5, scene 8](#/read/peer-gynt/a5s8:91). Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 85–86, and *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 439.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: extended metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another, with the likeness carried on part by part
lenses.why: Peer calls himself an onion and gives each coat the name of a man he has been; where he looks for a kernel, no man is named. Auden says almost everything Peer does is a part he plays.
lenses.caption: Peer tells himself he is an onion, not that he is like one. He carries the likeness on: the outermost layer is the shipwrecked man, then the passenger, then the gold-digger. A metaphor carried on like this is an extended metaphor. The marks pair each coat with its man. From swathings on, the onion words stand alone: where Peer looks for a kernel, he names nobody. In Act 4 he throws off a Turkish costume with a line that begins like the first coat’s, there lies the Turk, then here stand I; that part, he says, was only a matter of clothes. For Auden, almost everything Peer does is a part he plays.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what Peer says in it. Metaphor and its longer forms as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines them, under *metaphor*, *conceit* and *allegory*. The Turkish costume: [Act 4, scene 9](#/read/peer-gynt/a4s9:1). Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 438.

lenses.caption: Kaiser, from Caesar, is the German for emperor; the Archers’ translation uses it for Ibsen’s kejser. In Act 1 Peer tells his mother he will be a king, a kaiser, and Auden says the only empire safe from everyone else is one’s own consciousness. Just before the passage Peer composes his epitaph as Kaiser of the beasts; the passage begins by taking the title back. One coat is an ego, Latin for I: Ibsen writes jeget, the I. Peer looks for a kernel, the seed or core, and finds swathings, wrappings, in Ibsen simply layers. The scene ends with his cry, on hearing Solveig sing, that here was his Kaiserdom.
lenses.stands: The Online Etymology Dictionary under *kaiser*, *ego*, *swathe* and *kernel*. The translators’ note on *Kaiser* at Act 4, scene 1. Ibsen’s words in the Oslo edition and in *Bokmålsordboka*. The boast: [Act 1, scene 1](#/read/peer-gynt/a1s1:144). The epitaph and the last line of the scene: [Act 5, scene 5](#/read/peer-gynt/a5s5:3). The crowning: [Act 4, scene 13](#/read/peer-gynt/a4s13:221). Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 437.

lenses.caption: This is Ibsen’s measure for most of the play, kept in the Archers’ translation without his rhymes: four beats, the syllables between them free. William Archer took it to be designed for variety and suppleness in dialogue, and found it fit for moving speech as well as comic. Each of the three coats shown takes two lines. In Ibsen each pair is a rhymed couplet, and a handbook of verse says the quick return of the rhyme makes a couplet one unit: a coat to a couplet. The last line shown is split by a stage direction, as in Ibsen: two beats, Peer throws the pieces away, two beats more.

lenses.plain: the same words at the head of line after line, or of phrase after phrase
lenses.why: Peer asks where he was, twice over, and Solveig names a place three times, each time with my; Auden counts her line as one more answer and says Ibsen does not decide whether that faith is well founded.
lenses.caption: Peer begins two lines with the same three words, Where was I. Solveig answers in three phrases, all built on two words, in my. Starting line after line, or phrase after phrase, with the same words is called anaphora. His where asks for a place; her in my gives three, each something of hers. Peer starts back, calls these juggling words, and tells her that she is herself the mother of the man who is there. She says she is. Auden counts her line among the answers to the play’s question, and says Ibsen does not decide whether that faith is well founded.

lenses.name: aposiopesis
lenses.plain: a sentence broken off in the middle, with the rest left unsaid
lenses.why: The Button-Moulder’s sentence stops before it says what will be seen at the last cross-road, and two lines later the play ends; Auden wrote in 1941 that Peer has him still to meet and that no answer is final.
lenses.caption: The Button-Moulder’s voice comes into Solveig’s lullaby with two lines. The second begins to say what will be seen at the last cross-road, And then we’ll see whether, and stops: I say no more. Breaking off in mid-sentence is called aposiopesis. Three times he has let Peer go on to the next cross-road; the third time he also breaks off, at but then. Solveig then sings louder; her two lines return in the opposite order, with dream added. Auden wrote in 1941 that a staging in which Peer dies here gets the play wrong: Solveig’s answer settles no more than the others, and Peer has the Button-Moulder still to meet.

auden.says: In an essay of 1941 Auden makes the trolls’ saying the motto of a closed society and the human saying the motto of the adult member of an open one. In *The Dyer’s Hand* he calls the trolls’ motto the motto of the animals. He gives the human saying as a command to be true to oneself. That is the wording of R. Farquharson Sharp’s Everyman translation, the edition named on his reading list for the course, in which the two commands differ by one word. The Archers’ translation, printed here, has *be thyself*. The Button-Moulder’s lines he quotes in 1962 are in the Archers’ words.

Stauffer (1941), pp. 130–31; “Balaam and His Ass” and “Genius & Apostle,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 110 and 439; *Peer Gynt*, translated by R. Farquharson Sharp, Everyman’s Library (1921), Act 2, scene 6

auden.says: In *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950) Auden quotes the troll king’s riddle and its answer, in the Everyman wording, and calls it a catechism. The prospect of putting off human nature and being a troll, he says, draws every man, and each keeps something back, as Peer does. He also quotes the Button-Moulder’s answer about being oneself beside Father Mapple’s sermon in *Moby-Dick*, and says the two say the same thing. Near the end he has the Button-Moulder wait for the artist at the next cross-roads, to ask whether he has become himself.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 85–86, 116–17 and 149

auden.says: Three times in *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden tells another scene from the troll hall. The troll king proposes a small operation on Peer’s eye that would make a true troll of him, and Peer refuses. He will gladly call a cow a lovely girl, but he will not be altered until he cannot tell which is which. Auden calls that keeping his humanity, which includes the power to lie. In “Genius & Apostle” the scene shows the poet, who pretends for the fun of it and knows his made-up worlds are made up.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” “The Prince’s Dog” and “Genius & Apostle,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 110, 194 and 438

auden.says: In *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden says that Solveig’s answer is Peer’s own belief said back to him, and that the price of being a poet may yet be the Button-Moulder’s casting-ladle. So far, he adds, Peer has been lucky in the women behind him. He takes the bond of mother and child in the play as a parable of a love that time does not touch and that nothing either one does can change. In 1946 he set the ending beside that of Goethe’s *Faust*, found Faust’s rescue unconvincing, and called Ibsen the more honest of the two, since *Peer Gynt* ends with the Button-Moulder warning Peer of another meeting.
auden.quote: Ibsen leaves in doubt the question whether this faith is justified or not.

caveats: Auden’s review of 1941, “The Wandering Jew,” and his essay of 1946, “K.’s Quest,” were read here only in the passages that a search of scanned copies brings up. The sentences this page reports from them were seen; the pages around them were not.

The English verse is William and Charles Archer’s. Auden set his class the Everyman translation by R. Farquharson Sharp, which words these passages differently: its saying for men is to be true to oneself, and that is the form Auden quotes.

What is said of Ibsen’s Norwegian rests on the first-edition text in the University of Oslo’s edition and on a dictionary of today’s Norwegian. The Norwegian is described, not printed, and matching Ibsen’s spellings of 1867 to today’s dictionary words is this page’s own step.

The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing of a free measure of four beats. Several lines can fairly be heard another way, and Solveig’s answer can be given a fourth beat by leaning on a small word.

Peer names no man for two of the nine coats. That the coat like a crown is the straw crown of the madhouse, and the black-streaked coat the trade in slaves, idols and missionaries, is inferred from what he says of each and from its place in the order.
open: Auden’s review of 1941 (“The Wandering Jew”) and his essay of 1946 (“K.’s Quest”) are not among the scans. The examiner saw the sentences used here only as the passages that exact-phrase searches of archive.org return from scanned copies (the New Republic issue of 10 February 1941, the Prose volume, three copies of The Kafka Problem), not the full texts. The page numbers in Prose, vol. II (110–13) are the research notes’; the page of the 1946 sentences inside the essay (pp. 47–52, from the book’s contents) is not pinned, and the notes say p. 49. The view of the piece leans on the review of 1941. “Criticism in a Mass Society” has now been read in the open scan of The Intent of the Critic (1941), pp. 130–31.
The scan of The Dyer’s Hand misprints two words of the sentence quoted in the view (p. 436). The sentence is given as the research notes give it, where it is marked as checked against the page.

The Oxford English Dictionary’s full entries are behind a paywall. Only its public summary pages were read (origin, earliest date). The senses and dates in the word lenses are from the Online Etymology Dictionary.

The Norwegian text is not shown, because the research notes list no out-of-copyright source for it. What is said about Ibsen’s words and rhymes was read in the University of Oslo’s edition online. The meanings were read in a dictionary of today’s Bokmål; matching Ibsen’s spellings of 1867 (Svøb, tyndt, Kjærnen) to today’s headwords (svøp, tynn, kjerne) is this reading’s own step.

Auden’s remark that the Norwegian language keeps the I and the self apart in two words is given by him as something he had been told. Bokmålsordboka has both nouns, jeg and selv, and explains each by the other, so the remark could not be confirmed there.

The examiner cut the poet’s reading of the coats Peer pulls off unnamed as Acts 1 to 3: nothing in the text says what they are. Two matches in the table of coats are still inferences and say “it appears”: the coat like a crown as the straw crown of the madhouse (Act 4, scene 13), and the black-streaked ninth coat as the trade Peer tells of in Act 4, scene 1. Peer names no man for either. The row “then several at once” now gives no part and no place, and the drawing follows.
In this free four-beat measure some lines can be heard more than one way. The other hearings are listed in notes.md, and no caption leans on a doubtful syllable.

The research notes and the book of 1941 disagree about which of two pieces has which wording of the two mottos. remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md (section 17(d), H17e and H17o) gives “Criticism in a Mass Society” a wording that the scan of The Intent of the Critic does not have; the wording the notes give to “Romantic or Free?” is the one printed in that book on pp. 130–31. Nothing in this reading depends on it. Another piece that quotes the essay should check it against the scan.

The research notes list one page of The Enchafèd Flood for this play (p. 107). The scan has three more places, which the examiner read and brought in: pp. 85–86, where Auden quotes the troll king’s riddle and the two sayings and says what the trolls’ word means, pp. 116–17, where he sets the Button-Moulder’s answer beside Father Mapple’s sermon, and p. 149, where the Button-Moulder waits for the artist at the next cross-roads. The second and third bear on the Moby-Dick piece as well, and the research notes could be brought up to date.

The artist’s notes (art.md, item 14) point out that in the Ending tab every mark falls on the six small lines set beside the passage. The examiner left the third passage as the poet built it; a fourth passage is not allowed, and the riddle and its answer have to stay the large lines for the other three tabs.
